red-averias-4saltos.title: The intranet won't load from pc1
red-averias-4saltos.briefing: Ticket: "The intranet won't open from workstation `pc1`: `curl http://web.lab` returns no page." The network has four machines in a row: `pc1` (lan `10.5.1.0/24`) — `r1` — `r2` (transit `10.5.12.0/24`) — `srv` (dmz `10.5.3.0/24`, the web server, `10.5.3.10`). Once everything works, `curl http://web.lab` from `pc1` must return "srv OK". Work bottom-up and hop by hop; every machine has its own root terminal.
hints: There is more than one fault, in different layers and on different machines: fixing one usually uncovers the next. Follow the path hop by hop: can pc1 reach out? Does ping reach each machine? Do the replies come back? Is the port open? Does the name resolve correctly?

Look in three places: pc1's route and whether its next hop exists (`ip route get`, `ip neigh`); whether packets reach srv but replies don't return (`tcpdump -nni` on srv) and the routers' routes; and whether nginx listens but something filters the port (`ss -ltn`, `nmap -p80`, `nft list ruleset`). Then, where the IP of `web.lab` comes from (`getent hosts`).

pc1 has a gateway that doesn't exist: the route must go via `10.5.1.1` (`ip route replace 10.5.0.0/16 via 10.5.1.1`). r2 doesn't know the way back to the lan: `ip route add 10.5.1.0/24 via 10.5.12.1`. srv drops port 80 with an nftables rule (`nft flush ruleset` or delete the rule by its handle). And in pc1's `/etc/hosts`, `web.lab` points to `10.5.3.100`: edit it with nano or vim (`sed -i` fails in a container).
red-averias-4saltos.solution_summary: Four faults in four layers: (1) `pc1`'s route used a gateway that doesn't exist (`ip neigh` showed FAILED) and must use `r1`; (2) `r2` had no return route to the lan, so requests reached `srv` and the replies were lost (`tcpdump` gives it away); (3) an nftables rule on `srv` dropped port 80 even though nginx was listening (`nmap` reported filtered); (4) `/etc/hosts` on `pc1` resolved `web.lab` to the wrong IP, and it beats any DNS because of the `nsswitch` order.
red-averias-4saltos.blind_alert: INCIDENT [NETWORK] · A workstation on the lan can't open the internal website; the server appears to be up.

red-rutas-basicas.title: Two LANs joined by a router
red-rutas-basicas.briefing: Set up routing so `cliente` can reach the web server on `web` through router `r1`. The `lan_c` network (10.6.1.0/24) joins `cliente` and `r1`; the `lan_s` network (10.6.2.0/24) joins `r1` and `web`. Addresses are already configured, but forwarding and routes are missing. Work on all three nodes as root: `cliente`, `r1`, and `web`.
red-rutas-basicas.blind_alert: REQUEST [NETWORK] · Configure routing between two LANs through a Linux router.
hints: Follow the path of a packet from `cliente` to `web`: does `cliente` know which gateway to send traffic that is not on its network to? Does `r1` have forwarding enabled between its interfaces? Does `web` know how to send packets back to the `cliente` network?

Look at the routing table on `cliente` and `web` (`ip route`, `ip route get`) and at the value of `sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward` on `r1`. Routes between networks are added with `ip route add <red> via <puerta>`; the gateway is the IP address of `r1` on each network.
On `r1`: `sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`. On `cliente`: `ip route add 10.6.2.0/24 via 10.6.1.1`. On `web`: `ip route add 10.6.1.0/24 via 10.6.2.1`.
red-rutas-basicas.solution_summary: The Linux kernel does not forward packets between interfaces when `ip_forward=0`, so `r1` drops packets that arrive from one network and are destined to the other. Each host only knows its local network; to reach the other network it needs an explicit route with the next hop. With forwarding enabled and both routes in place, the round trip works.

red-nat-nftables.title: NAT and firewall with nftables
red-nat-nftables.briefing: On `fw`, configure outbound NAT (masquerade) toward the `wan` network and a firewall that only allows outbound HTTP traffic from `pc1`; ICMP ping must be blocked. `pc1` is on `lan` (10.7.1.0/24), `fw` joins `lan` and `wan` (10.7.2.0/24), and `ext` is the web server on `wan`. Addresses and forwarding are already configured. Work on `fw` and test from `pc1`.
red-nat-nftables.blind_alert: REQUEST [NETWORK] · Configure NAT and firewall so a LAN can reach the Internet only over HTTP.
hints: Traffic from `pc1` to `ext` leaves `fw` with the private LAN source address; `ext` doesn't know how to send replies back. You need to translate the source address as it exits `wan` and let conntrack track the connection.

With nftables: an `ip nat` table with a `postrouting` chain (type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat) and a rule `oifname "eth1" masquerade`. Then an `inet filtro` table with a `forward` chain (policy drop), a rule `ct state established,related accept`, and a rule for TCP destination port 80 from `lan` to `wan`. With iptables: `iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth1 -j MASQUERADE`, `iptables -P FORWARD DROP`, `iptables -A FORWARD -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT`, `iptables -A FORWARD -i eth0 -o eth1 -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT`.

Concrete commands with nftables: `nft add table ip nat; nft add chain ip nat postrouting '{ type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; }'; nft add rule ip nat postrouting oifname "eth1" masquerade; nft add table inet filtro; nft add chain inet filtro forward '{ type filter hook forward priority filter; policy drop; }'; nft add rule inet filtro forward ct state established,related accept; nft add rule inet filtro forward iifname "eth0" oifname "eth1" tcp dport 80 accept`.
red-nat-nftables.solution_summary: Without NAT, `ext` receives packets with source 10.7.1.10 and has no return route; masquerade changes the source to 10.7.2.1, so `ext` replies to `fw` and conntrack undoes the translation. The firewall with a drop policy on forward only allows already-established connections and outbound HTTP, blocking ICMP ping.

red-ospf-frr.title: OSPF with FRR between three routers
red-ospf-frr.briefing: Configure OSPF on routers `r1`, `r2`, and `r3` (area 0) so the `h1` LAN (10.8.1.0/24) and `h3` LAN (10.8.3.0/24) can see each other. Host addresses and routing are already configured; the routers have their interfaces and forwarding, but they do not know routes to the remote LANs. FRR is installed but stopped; you must configure and start it. Work on the routers in `vtysh` mode or by editing `/etc/frr/frr.conf`; use `h1` and `h3` for testing.
red-ospf-frr.blind_alert: REQUEST [NETWORK] · Configure OSPF on three routers so the LANs converge.
hints: OSPF needs `ospfd` to be enabled in `/etc/frr/daemons` and the configuration (`/etc/frr/frr.conf`) to declare the networks in area 0. Each router must advertise its directly connected networks.

In `vtysh`: `conf t`, `router ospf`, `network <red> area 0`, `passive-interface` on the host-facing LANs. Restart with `/usr/lib/frr/frrinit.sh start`. To check, `show ip ospf neighbor` should show state `Full` and `show ip route ospf` should show routes with code `O`.

Minimal configuration: on `r1`, networks 10.8.1.0/24, 10.8.12.0/30, 10.8.13.0/30; on `r2`, 10.8.12.0/30, 10.8.23.0/30; on `r3`, 10.8.3.0/24, 10.8.13.0/30, 10.8.23.0/30. All in area 0; on r1 and r3, `passive-interface` on the host LAN interface (eth0 on r1, eth2 on r3).
red-ospf-frr.solution_summary: OSPF propagates routes by exchanging LSAs: if the three routers declare their directly connected networks in area 0, they establish adjacencies (Full state) and each one computes the shortest path. Host LANs are advertised passively (no Hello on that interface). The hosts do not participate in OSPF; they only need their local route to the router.

red-otra-interfaz.title: Reach a service through another interface
red-otra-interfaz.briefing: The systems team says `app`'s metrics (port 9100) listen only on the management IP (10.9.2.10), and that is why the corporate network cannot reach them. You are on `dev`, on the corporate network (10.9.1.0/24). On `dev`, configure what is needed so `curl http://10.9.2.10:9100/metrics` returns the metrics, without touching `app` or `mon`. `dev` already has its IP and can see `app` via its corporate IP 10.9.1.10; `mon` is at 10.9.2.20.
red-otra-interfaz.blind_alert: REQUEST [NETWORK] · Make a service that only listens on the management IP reachable from the corporate network.
hints: In Linux an IP address belongs to the host, not to the interface: the kernel accepts a packet for any of its local IP addresses even if it arrives on another NIC (weak host model). So ask yourself why packets from `dev` to the management IP don't even leave toward `app`.

On `dev`, look at the chosen route with `ip route get 10.9.2.10`; for a single host, add a /32 route with `ip route add <ip>/32 via <ip_corporativa_de_app>`. The gateway must be on the same network as `dev`.
Concrete command on `dev`: `ip route add 10.9.2.10/32 via 10.9.1.10`. Then `curl http://10.9.2.10:9100/metrics` should return the metrics.
red-otra-interfaz.solution_summary: Linux's weak host model (RFC 1122) makes the kernel treat its IP addresses as belonging to the host, not to each interface. By adding a /32 route on `dev` toward `app`'s management IP using its corporate IP as the next hop, the packet reaches `app` through its corporate interface and, since the destination is local, it is delivered to the process listening on 10.9.2.10:9100. There is no need to enable `ip_forward` on `app`.
